steps.say: Linux is an open-source operating system used across servers, cloud infrastructure and development environments.
Many DevOps tools, including Docker and Kubernetes, commonly run on Linux.
The terminal gives direct control of the system, which makes Linux an essential skill on remote servers.
The terminal is a text window where you type commands instead of clicking.
The shell reads the command and asks the operating system to carry it out.
The result comes back as plain text in the same window.
Because commands are just text, they can be saved and automated later.

auto.text: Commands can be saved and repeated

steps.say: Linux organizes everything in a single tree that starts at the root directory, written /.
User files live in /home.
term: bin  etc  home  tmp  usr  var

steps.say: /etc holds configuration, while /var holds logs and application data.
/tmp is for temporary files. Every file in the system hangs from the one root.
Every file has a path. Here the current directory is /home/student.
An absolute path starts at / and walks down from the top of the tree.
A relative path starts from where you are now, so it is usually shorter.
.. means the parent directory and ~ means your home directory.

subtopics.title: Navigate with pwd, ls and cd

steps.say: pwd prints the directory you are in right now.
ls -la lists everything here, including hidden files and permissions.
cd projects moves you into that directory.
cd .. goes back up one level, and cd ~ always takes you home.
mkdir -p creates a directory together with any missing parent directories.
One command created the whole path: projects and projects/linux now exist.
touch creates a new, empty file.
Directories keep your work organised; files hold the content.
A project file, notes.txt, sits in the current directory next to an empty projects folder.
cp makes a copy. The original stays where it was.
mv moves a file, here into the projects directory.
mv also renames: it is the same file under a new name.
Two things to clean up: a file, and a directory that contains another file.
rm deletes a file. There is no recycle bin, so it generally cannot be undone.
rm -r removes a directory and everything inside it.
Always double-check the path before pressing Enter.

chk.text: Verify the path before you delete

subtopics.title: Read Files: cat, less, head and tail

steps.say: cat prints a whole file to the terminal in one go.
less opens a long file one page at a time: Space for next page, q to quit.
head shows the first lines of a file; -n 5 limits it to five.
tail shows the end of a file; -f keeps following new lines as they arrive.
Large log files make problems hard to spot by eye.
grep prints only the lines that match. -i ignores upper and lower case.
grep -r searches every file in a directory, here for the word database.
Linux is multi-user: every user has an identity, and users can belong to groups.
Every file has an owner and an associated group.
Permissions then decide what the owner, the group and everyone else may do.
ls -l prints a string of ten characters for every file, for example -rwxr-xr--.
The first character is the file type. The next nine form three groups: owner, group and others.
In each group r means read, w means write and x means execute. A dash means that permission is missing.
Here the owner can read, write and run; the group can read and run; others can only read.
Each permission has a number: read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1.
Add the values for each class: rwx is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, while r-x is 4 + 0 + 1 = 5.
Three digits give owner, group and others. 755 means rwxr-xr-x and 644 means rw-r--r--.
deploy.sh was just created, so it is readable but not executable.
chmod u+x adds execute permission for the owner (u = user, g = group, o = others).

lg.text: u = owner · g = group · o = others

steps.say: Numeric mode sets all three classes at once: 755 gives rwxr-xr-x.
644 is a common choice for regular files: the owner edits, everyone else reads.
Every file belongs to one owner and one group. Here notes.txt belongs to root.
chown changes ownership. It needs elevated rights, so it is run with sudo.
The pattern is chown owner:group file.
root is the all-powerful administrator account. Regular users have limited rights.
Without sudo, a regular user is denied access to protected files.
term: !E: Could not open lock file - Permission denied

steps.say: sudo runs a single command with root privileges for users who are authorized.
Elevated commands can change or delete protected files, so verify every command and path first.
Whenever a program runs, Linux creates a process and gives it a unique Process ID (PID).

pd.text: Every process gets its own PID

steps.say: ps aux takes a snapshot of every running process.
top shows CPU and memory usage live and keeps refreshing.
A frozen program keeps its PID but no longer responds.
kill sends a polite request to stop. The process gets a chance to shut down cleanly.
If the process ignores the request, it keeps running.
kill -9 forces termination immediately. Use it only when necessary: nothing is cleaned up.
Services are background programs: web hosting, database access, remote connections.
On systems that use systemd, services are managed with systemctl.
systemctl status reports whether a service is running.
term: ● nginx.service - A high performance web server

subtopics.title: Start, Stop and Restart a Service

steps.say: A service is either running or stopped. nginx is stopped right now.
start launches the service.
stop shuts it down.
restart stops and starts it again, for example to load new configuration.

subtopics.title: Start Now vs Start at Boot

steps.say: Starting a service only changes its current state.
systemctl start turns it on now, but it will not come back after a reboot.
systemctl enable configures automatic startup during system boot.
After a reboot, an enabled service starts again on its own.

ok.text: After reboot: nginx is running again

steps.say: systemd collects the output of every service in one place: the journal.
journalctl -u nginx shows the logs of one service.
-n 20 limits the output to the 20 most recent entries.
-f follows the log and prints new messages as they arrive.
nginx stopped working. Start with its status.
Then read the recent logs to find the reason.
Fix the cause (free port 80), restart the service and confirm it is running.
An IP address identifies a device or network interface.
A port identifies a communication endpoint on that device: SSH uses 22, HTTP 80 and HTTPS 443.
DNS translates a domain name into an IP address, so you never need to remember numbers.
ping sends a small request to a host to see whether it answers.
A reply means the host is reachable. -c 4 stops after four requests.
No reply can mean the host is down, blocked by a firewall or unreachable.
curl fetches a URL and prints what comes back: ideal for testing websites and APIs.
curl -I asks only for the response headers, such as the status code.
Point curl at localhost to check that your own backend is answering.
ss -tuln lists the TCP and UDP ports that are listening for connections.
With sudo and -p, ss also shows which process owns each port.
If your app is missing from the list, it is not listening on its expected port.

subtopics.title: Connect to a Server with SSH

steps.say: Secure Shell (SSH) opens an encrypted connection to a remote Linux machine, usually on port 22.
The connection is encrypted, so commands and passwords cannot be read on the way.
From now on, every command you type runs on the remote server.
ssh-keygen creates a key pair: a private key and a matching public key.
ssh-copy-id installs the public key on the server.
Now the private key proves who you are: no password needed.
The private key must stay secret and should never be committed to GitHub.
A package manager installs, updates and removes software, and takes care of dependencies.
Ubuntu and Debian use apt. Red Hat-based systems use dnf, or yum on older ones.
The available package manager depends on your distribution: check it first.

subtopics.title: Install, Update and Remove with apt

steps.say: Your system keeps a list of available packages. Right now it is out of date.
sudo apt update refreshes the package list from the repository.
sudo apt install downloads nginx and the dependencies it needs.
sudo apt upgrade brings installed packages up to date.
sudo apt remove uninstalls a package you no longer need.

subtopics.title: apt vs dnf: Same Idea, Different Command

steps.say: On Red Hat-based systems the same tasks are done with dnf instead of apt.
Install, update and remove map one-to-one, so only the command name changes.
nano opens a simple text editor inside the terminal, handy on remote servers.
Type directly into the file. Here the port changes from 8080 to 9090.
Ctrl + O saves ("writes out") the file.
Ctrl + X leaves nano and returns you to the shell.
Vim is a modal editor: what a key does depends on the mode. It starts in Normal mode.
Press i to enter Insert mode, where typing changes the text.
Press Esc to go back to Normal mode.
From Normal mode, colon commands save and quit.
A script is a text file of commands. It begins with a shebang that names the interpreter.
chmod +x makes the script executable.
Now ./hello.sh runs it and prints the message.
Variables store values that you can reuse inside a script.
echo reads the variable with $name and prints its value.
Command-line arguments such as $1 and $2 let users give different input on each run.
Run it again with another value and the same script gives a different result.
Conditions let a script decide what to do. This one checks whether config.txt exists.
When the file exists, the test succeeds and the if branch runs.
Remove the file and the else branch runs instead.
A for loop repeats the same commands for each value in a list.

p.title: loop.sh
lines: for item in Git Linux Docker

steps.say: First pass: item is Git, so the loop prints Learning: Git.
Second pass: item becomes Linux.
Third pass: Docker. After the last value the loop ends by itself.
backup.sh takes a project directory as its argument and copies it to a timestamped backup folder.
The script stops with a usage message when the argument is missing or not a directory.
It creates the backup root and builds a name from the current date and time.
cp -r copies the project, and the script reports success or failure.

subtopics.title: Mini Project: Run and Verify the Backup

steps.say: Create a sample project, then make backup.sh executable.
Run the script with the project as its argument. A timestamped copy appears in ~/backups.
Each execution creates a separate backup, so earlier copies are never overwritten.
Without a valid directory, the script prints its usage message and exits.
